summary: Specifies the combinations of security mechanisms that are required and recommended in LDAP implementations for authentication. It is on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 4510 and RFC 4513.

plainLanguage.summary: LDAP is the protocol that lets a program look things up in a directory. This RFC says which ways of proving who you are a directory server has to accept, so that any client can authenticate with any server: no password, a password protected by a digest, a plain password inside an encrypted connection, or a client certificate.

subtitle: Which ways of proving who you are an LDAP server must accept.

tldr.problem: LDAP version 3 offers searching, fetching and manipulating directory content, and the security functions that go with it. For those to work across the Internet they have to be interoperable, and each implementation choosing for itself would mean clients that cannot talk to any server.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists the threats to a directory service, then states which security mechanisms are required and which are recommended: anonymous access, password authentication with DIGEST-MD5, a simple password bind over TLS, and authentication with a client certificate.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2829 is a Proposed Standard from May 2000 and has been obsoleted by RFC 4510 and RFC 4513, which cover the protocol and its authentication.

today: RFC 2829 is a Proposed Standard from May 2000, and it has been obsoleted by RFC 4510 and RFC 4513, which cover the LDAP protocol and its authentication mechanisms; the unit metadata also lists RFC 3377 as updating it. The RFC itself states that it specifies particular combinations of security mechanisms that are required and recommended in LDAP implementations.

sections.title: The Threats to a Directory Service
sections.content:
LDAP version 3 is a powerful access protocol for directories. It offers ways of searching, fetching and manipulating directory content, and ways of reaching the rich set of security functions built into the protocol. For the Internet to work, those security functions have to be interoperable, so there has to be a minimum subset that every implementation claiming LDAPv3 conformance supports.

The RFC lists seven basic threats. Hostile clients account for unauthorized access to data through fetch operations, unauthorized modification of data, unauthorized modification of configuration, and unauthorized or excessive use of resources. Hostile agents on the path between client and server, or posing as the server, account for unauthorized access to reusable client authentication information by watching others' access, unauthorized access to data by watching others' access, and spoofing of the directory, where a client is tricked into believing information came from the directory when it did not.

The protocol suite can be protected with six kinds of mechanism: client authentication using the SASL mechanism set, possibly backed by the TLS credentials exchange; client authorization through access control based on the requester's authenticated identity; data integrity protection through TLS or data-integrity SASL mechanisms; protection against snooping through TLS or data-encrypting SASL mechanisms; resource limitation through administrative limits on service controls; and server authentication through TLS or a SASL mechanism. At the time of writing, access controls were imposed by means outside the scope of the LDAP protocol itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Two kinds of attacker are in scope: a client that tries too much, and someone on the network who watches or redirects. The RFC lists what can be used against each, then says which of those tools every implementation has to have.

sections.title: Authentication, Credentials and Identity
sections.content:
An access control policy is a set of rules defining the protection of resources, generally in terms of the capabilities of the people or entities accessing them. A common expression of one is an access control list. The RFC notes that imposing access controls was still done by means outside the scope of the LDAP protocol.

While a request is being processed, the server may associate it with a range of security-related factors, which it calls access control factors. These might include the source IP address, the encryption strength, the type of operation requested, or the time of day. Some belong to the request, some to the connection it arrived on, and some are environmental. Access control policies are expressed in terms of these factors, and the set the server makes available is implementation-specific.

Authentication credentials are the evidence one party supplies to another, asserting the identity of the party supplying it. Authentication is the process of generating, transmitting and verifying those credentials and the identity they assert, and an authentication identity is the name presented in a credential. Credentials take many forms depending on the mechanism negotiated: X.509 certificates, Kerberos tickets, or a simple identity and password pair. A mechanism may constrain the form of identity used with it.

An authorization identity is the name of the user or entity asking for an operation to be performed, and it is one kind of access control factor. The authorization identity bound to an association is often exactly the authentication identity the client presented, but it may differ: SASL lets a client name an authorization identity distinct from the one its credentials assert, so that a proxy server can authenticate with its own credentials while requesting the privileges of the identity it proxies for. How a server composes and validates an authorization identity from the credentials a client supplies is implementation-specific.
sections.plainLanguage: Two names are in play for a client: the one its credentials prove, and the one it wants to be treated as. They are usually the same, but a proxy needs them to differ. The RFC also introduces the idea of access control factors, the things a server can take into account when deciding whether to allow an operation.

sections.title: The Required Security Mechanisms
sections.content:
The RFC argues that letting each implementation pick and choose among the alternatives is not a strategy likely to lead to interoperability. Without mandates, clients get written that support no security function the server supports, or worse, support only cleartext passwords. It also notes that active intermediary attacks are the hardest for an attacker to perform and the hardest for an implementation to defend against, and that methods protecting only against hostile clients and passive eavesdropping are still useful where the perceived risk does not justify the cost.

Three implementation conformance requirements follow. For a read-only public directory, anonymous authentication can be used. Implementations offering password-based authenticated access must support authentication with the DIGEST-MD5 SASL mechanism, which gives client authentication with protection against passive eavesdropping but not against active intermediary attacks. For a directory needing session protection and authentication, the Start TLS extended operation together with either the simple authentication choice or the SASL EXTERNAL mechanism is to be used; implementations should support a password and should support a certificate, and together these give integrity and disclosure protection and authentication of both client and server, including against active intermediary attacks.

Two rules about discarding earlier information follow. If TLS is negotiated, the client must discard everything it learned about the server beforehand, because the list of supported SASL mechanisms may change once TLS is in place, with EXTERNAL and PLAIN likely to be listed only afterwards. If a SASL security layer is negotiated, the client must discard what it learned before SASL, and a client configured to support several SASL mechanisms should fetch the supported list both before and after, and check that it has not changed. That detects an active attack that removes mechanisms from the list, and it lets the client be sure it is using the best mechanism both ends support.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says plainly: pick one, or nothing will interoperate. Three things are required or recommended, and everything a client learned about the server before the connection was protected has to be thrown away, because an attacker could have planted it.

sections.title: Anonymous and Password-Based Authentication
sections.content:
Directory operations that modify entries or reach protected attributes generally require client authentication. Clients that intend to do none of those typically use anonymous authentication, which every LDAP implementation must support. A client that has not completed a bind operation on a connection is anonymously authenticated, and a client may also ask for anonymous authentication explicitly by sending a zero-length string with the simple authentication choice. A server should let an anonymously bound client retrieve the supportedSASLMechanisms attribute of the root DSE, and may use other information about the client to grant or deny access even to anonymous ones.

For passwords, implementations must support the DIGEST-MD5 SASL mechanism. The client can find out whether the server supports it by searching the root DSE for the supportedSASLMechanisms attribute and looking for the string DIGEST-MD5. The first stage is a bind request with the mechanism named and no credentials; the server replies with a bind response whose result code is saslBindInProgress and whose server credentials carry a digest challenge, which should include a realm and must indicate support for UTF-8. The client then sends a second bind request with a distinct message id carrying the digest response, whose service type is ldap. The server answers with success or an error.

Implementations should also support the simple authentication choice when the connection is protected against eavesdropping using TLS. The client uses the Start TLS operation to negotiate TLS, which need not come before a bind. For the procedure to succeed, both sides must negotiate a cipher suite with a bulk encryption algorithm of appropriate strength. After the TLS negotiation the client sends a bind request with the name of the user's entry and the simple authentication choice containing a password, and the server compares it, case-sensitively, with each value of the userPassword attribute in the named entry, answering with success or invalidCredentials.
sections.plainLanguage: Anonymous access means proving nothing at all. For a password there are two routes: one where the password never crosses the wire in the clear, and one where it crosses inside an encrypted connection. The RFC requires the first and recommends the second.

sections.title: Certificate-Based Authentication
sections.content:
Implementations should support authentication with a client certificate carried in TLS. A user whose public key has been signed by a certification authority may authenticate with that key pair if the server requests the user's certificate. The certificate's subject field should be the name of the user's directory entry, and the certification authority must be trusted enough by the directory server for the server to process the certificate. How servers validate certificate paths is outside the scope of the document.

A server may support mappings for certificates whose subject field differs from the user's directory entry, but a server that supports such mappings must also be configurable to handle certificates that need no mapping. The client uses the Start TLS operation to negotiate TLS. In the negotiation the server must request a certificate, the client provides it, and the client must perform a private-key operation to prove it holds the matching private key.

Because deployments will need to protect sensitive data in transit, the client and server must negotiate a cipher suite with a bulk encryption algorithm of appropriate strength. The server must verify that the client's certificate is valid, normally by checking that it was issued by a known authority and that no certificate on the client's chain is invalid or revoked. After the TLS negotiation the client sends a bind request using the SASL EXTERNAL mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: A client that holds a certificate signed by a trusted authority can prove who it is by completing the TLS handshake with that certificate. The server then checks the certificate and the client binds with the EXTERNAL mechanism to say which identity it wants to use.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says security issues are discussed throughout, and that the unsurprising conclusion is that mandatory security is important and that session encryption is required when snooping is a problem.

Servers are encouraged to prevent modifications by anonymous users, and may wish to reduce denial of service attacks by timing out idle connections and returning the unwillingToPerform result code rather than performing computationally expensive operations requested by unauthorized clients. A connection on which the client has neither performed the Start TLS operation nor negotiated a suitable SASL mechanism for integrity and encryption is open to man-in-the-middle attacks on the traffic in transit.

The RFC also lists cipher suite guidance. Three suites must not be used for confidentiality protection of passwords or data: TLS_NULL_WITH_NULL_NULL, TLS_RSA_WITH_NULL_MD5 and TLS_RSA_WITH_NULL_SHA. Nine suites can be cracked in less than a week of CPU time on a standard CPU in 1997, so both ends should consider the value of what they are protecting before using them. Five suites are vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks and should not be used to protect passwords or sensitive data unless the network configuration makes the danger tolerable. A client or server that supports TLS must support at least TLS_DHE_DSS_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA.
sections.plainLanguage: The advice is that a connection with no protection at all is open to interception, and that anonymous clients should not be allowed to change things. The RFC also names the cipher suites that must not be used, those that are breakable, and the weakest one that is still acceptable.

items.label: Must support
items.desc: Every implementation must support anonymous authentication. A client that has not bound is anonymously authenticated.

items.label: Must support
items.desc: Implementations offering password-based authenticated access must support it. It protects against passive eavesdropping but not against active intermediary attacks.

items.label: Should support
items.desc: A password sent inside a TLS-protected connection. It is not suitable where there is no network or transport layer confidentiality.

items.label: Should support
items.desc: Used with the Start TLS operation. Without an established TLS session or another external source of credentials, the bind must fail with inappropriateAuthentication.

items.label: Not used
items.desc: Not used with LDAP, because LDAP already has a native anonymous authentication method.

items.label: Not used
items.desc: Not used with LDAP, because LDAP already has a native plaintext authentication method.
